implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the one-shot awaitable, so the correlation table stores a std::promise<Reply> per id and the caller waits on the paired std::future with wait_for(deadline); the reader thread looks the id up, satisfies the promise with set_value or set_exception and erases the entry. Only the table, the id generation and the wire field stay hand-written - and the promise half must stay in the table because a std::future cannot be completed from the outside. Take this variant when no async framework is available or a dependency-free build matters.
pitfalls: A std::promise can be satisfied only once: a duplicate reply throws std::future_error, so extract or erase the entry under the lock and drop late replies instead of calling set_value again.
wait_for returning ready also covers a broken promise or an attached exception - always call get() and let it propagate, otherwise failures look like successes.
Destroying an unsatisfied promise makes the paired future fail with broken_promise, so a timeout path that erases the promise must not leave a caller believing its future is still live.
Never hold the table mutex while waiting: the reader thread needs it to deliver, so wait on the future outside the lock.

variants.name: Boost.Asio awaitable coroutines over one connection
variants.idiom_name: co_await async_read/async_write (use_awaitable) + awaitable_operators for the deadline
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 coroutines and Boost.Asio the requestor's code becomes linear: a single demultiplexing coroutine reads each frame, extracts the correlation id and resumes the waiter held in the per-connection table, while the caller awaits with co_await and expresses its deadline through awaitable_operators (for example co_await (async_read(...) || timer.async_wait(use_awaitable))). The identifier and the table do not disappear - only the callback plumbing around them does. Choose this variant when the toolchain is C++20 and the callback pyramid is the real cost; the promise/future table remains the smaller, dependency-free option.
pitfalls: The demultiplexer and the waiters must share one table; giving each request its own read coroutine reintroduces a reader per request and lets concurrent reads steal each other's replies.
Forget as_tuple()/redirect_error and the error_code is turned into a thrown system_error at the co_await, so a missing reply looks like a transport failure.
Awaitable state lives on the coroutine frame: erasing a pending entry while its coroutine is still suspended on it leaves a frame nobody ever resumes.
